subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Why is the second ionisation energy of any element always greater than its first?
options: The second electron is removed from a larger atom
Shielding increases after the first electron is removed
The second electron is removed from a positive ion, so it is held more strongly by the same nuclear charge over fewer electrons
The nuclear charge increases after ionisation
questions.explain: After the first electron leaves, the remaining electrons are pulled in by an unchanged nuclear charge with reduced repulsion, so more energy is needed.

questions.q: What does the existence of successive ionisation energies that fall into distinct groups (e.g. 2, then 8, then 8) provide evidence for?
options: The nuclear model of the atom
The arrangement of electrons in shells (energy levels)
questions.explain: Clusters of successive ionisation energies separated by large jumps are direct evidence that electrons occupy distinct shells.

questions.q: How many electrons can be held in total by a complete set of d orbitals in one sub-shell?
questions.explain: A d sub-shell contains five orbitals, each holding two electrons, giving a maximum of ten.

questions.q: During electron impact ionisation in a mass spectrometer, what happens to the sample particles?
options: They are accelerated without any charge change
A high-energy electron knocks out an electron, forming a 1+ positive ion
They are split into protons and neutrons
They gain an electron to form negative ions
questions.explain: A high-energy electron from an electron gun knocks an electron off each particle, typically forming 1+ ions.

questions.q: Which statement about sub-atomic particles is correct on the relative-mass scale where a proton = 1?
options: A neutron carries a relative charge of -1
A proton and electron have equal but opposite relative masses
A neutron has a relative mass of 1 and a relative charge of 0
An electron has a relative mass of exactly 0
questions.explain: A neutron has relative mass 1 and is uncharged, whereas an electron has relative mass ~1/1836 (often approximated to 0 but not exactly zero).

questions.q: In time-of-flight mass spectrometry, why must samples be ionised before detection?
options: To remove the neutrons from the sample
To increase the mass of the particles
So that the particles can be accelerated by an electric field and create a current on detection
questions.explain: Ions are needed so they can be accelerated by an electric field and so that they generate a measurable current when they strike the detector.

questions.q: Chlorine has two isotopes: 35Cl (75.0%) and 37Cl (25.0%). What is its relative atomic mass?
What is the full electron configuration of a chromium atom (Z = 24) in its ground state?
questions.explain: Chromium adopts 3d5 4s1 because a half-filled d sub-shell with a singly-occupied 4s gives extra stability.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are there in a ground-state nitrogen atom (Z = 7)?
questions.explain: Nitrogen is 1s2 2s2 2p3, and the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals singly, giving three unpaired electrons.

questions.q: What is the main reason first ionisation energy generally decreases down a group?
options: The outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and more shielded, despite increased nuclear charge
Electron-electron repulsion decreases down the group
Nuclear charge decreases down the group
questions.explain: Down a group the outer electron occupies a higher principal energy level and experiences more shielding, so it is held less strongly even though nuclear charge rises.

questions.q: In which block of the periodic table is the element with configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4?
questions.explain: The highest-energy electrons are in the 3p sub-shell, placing the element (sulfur) in the p-block.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy a single atomic orbital, and why?
options: Ten, the capacity of a d sub-shell
Eight, to satisfy the octet rule
Two, because the Pauli exclusion principle requires opposite spins
questions.explain: An orbital holds at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins according to the Pauli exclusion principle.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
options: Oxygen has more shielding shells than nitrogen
Oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge
In oxygen the paired 2p electrons repel, making one easier to remove than nitrogen's half-filled 2p set
questions.explain: Oxygen has two electrons paired in one 2p orbital; the resulting electron-electron repulsion makes removal easier than from nitrogen's stable half-filled p sub-shell.

questions.q: Which element is found in the d-block of the periodic table?
questions.explain: Vanadium fills its 3d sub-shell and so lies in the d-block, whereas Ca is s-block and Al/Si are p-block.

questions.q: Which sub-shell is filled immediately after the 3p sub-shell when building up electron configurations?
questions.explain: 4s is at a lower energy than 3d in the filling sequence, so 4s fills before 3d.

questions.q: In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer, two ions are accelerated to the same kinetic energy. Which reaches the detector first?
options: The ion with the smaller mass
Both arrive at the same time
The ion with the greater charge always arrives first regardless of mass
The ion with the larger mass
questions.explain: For equal kinetic energy, the lighter ion has a greater velocity and so a shorter time of flight.

questions.q: A sample of magnesium gives mass-spectrum peaks at m/z = 24, 25 and 26 with abundances 79.0%, 10.0% and 11.0%. What is the relative atomic mass to 1 d.p.?
Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium, against the general trend across a period?
options: Boron has a half-filled 2p sub-shell that is destabilised
Boron has fewer protons than beryllium
Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital of slightly higher energy than the 2s electron removed from beryllium
questions.explain: The first electron removed from boron is a 2p electron, which is at a higher energy and less tightly held than beryllium's 2s electron.

questions.q: Which statement about the 4s and 3d sub-shells is correct?
options: 4s fills first and 3d empties first on ionisation
4s fills first but 4s empties first on ionisation
questions.explain: 4s fills before 3d during the build-up, yet 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons when the atom is ionised.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of an Fe2+ ion (Fe is Z = 26)?
questions.explain: When transition metals ionise, the 4s electrons are lost before any 3d electrons, giving Fe2+ as [Ar] 3d6.

questions.q: How many electrons in total can the third principal energy level (n = 3) hold?
questions.explain: n = 3 contains 3s (2), 3p (6) and 3d (10) sub-shells, holding 18 electrons in total.

questions.q: Which ion has the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 (i.e. that of argon)?
questions.explain: Ca2+ (Z = 20, losing two electrons) has 18 electrons giving the argon configuration; Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ all have the neon configuration.

questions.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
questions.explain: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical about the nucleus.

questions.q: The successive ionisation energies of an element show a large jump between the 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies. In which group does the element lie?
questions.explain: A big jump after two electrons are removed shows the third electron comes from an inner, closer shell, identifying a Group 2 element.

questions.q: Which Cu electron configuration is correct, reflecting the stability of a full d sub-shell?
questions.explain: Copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1 because a completely full 3d sub-shell with a single 4s electron is energetically favourable.

questions.q: What is the relative charge and relative mass of an electron (to the usual approximation)?
questions.explain: An electron has a relative charge of -1 and a relative mass of about 1/1836 of a proton.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of a molecule, which peak corresponds to the molecular ion?
options: The peak at the lowest m/z value
The peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring isotope peaks), equal to the relative molecular mass
questions.explain: The molecular ion peak is the one at the highest m/z (the M peak), and its value equals the relative molecular mass.

questions.q: How many orbitals are present in a p sub-shell, and what shape are they?
questions.explain: A p sub-shell has three dumb-bell-shaped orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles to each other.

questions.q: Which principle states that electrons fill orbitals singly before pairing up?
questions.explain: Hund's rule states that orbitals of equal energy are each occupied singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing occurs.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of bromine (Br2) shows molecular ion peaks at m/z = 158, 160 and 162. This pattern arises because:
options: Bromine has a relative atomic mass of 160
Bromine has three isotopes of equal abundance
Br2 contains two atoms each of which can be 79Br or 81Br, giving combinations of 158, 160 and 162
questions.explain: With two roughly equally abundant isotopes (79Br and 81Br), Br2 gives 79+79=158, 79+81=160 and 81+81=162 in a 1:2:1 ratio.
